title: Ἀετὸς καὶ κολοιὸς καὶ ποιμήν
titleEn: The Eagle, the Jackdaw, and the Shepherd
part: The Eagle, the Jackdaw, and the Shepherd (Chambry 5 · Perry 2)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 5 (= Perry 2). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἀετὸς καταπτὰς ἀπό τινος ὑψηλῆς πέτρας ἄρνα ἥρπασε· κολοιὸς δὲ τοῦτο θεασάμενος διὰ ζῆλον τοῦτον μιμήσασθαι ἠθέλησε· καὶ δὴ καθεὶς ἑαυτὸν μετὰ πολλοῦ ῥοίζου ἐπὶ κριὸν ἠνέχθη.
sentences.tr: Aetos kataptas apo tinos hypsēlēs petras arna hērpase· koloios de touto theasamenos dia zēlon touton mimēsasthai ēthelēse· kai dē katheis heauton meta pollou rhoizou epi krion ēnechthē.
sentences.l: An eagle, having swooped down from a certain high rock, snatched up a lamb; and a jackdaw, having seen this, out of emulation wished to imitate him; and so, having let himself down with a great whirring, he was carried against a ram.
sentences.i: An eagle swooped down from a high rock and carried off a lamb; a jackdaw, seeing it, was seized with emulation and wanted to do the same; so he launched himself with a great rush of wings and bore down on a ram.
sentences.n: ζῆλος is emulation shading into envy — the wish to match someone above you, which is what the whole fable is about. ῥοῖζος is the whistling rush of something moving fast through the air; an initial ῥ always carries the rough breathing, romanized rh. ἠνέχθη is the aorist passive of φέρω; φέρομαι in the passive is the ordinary Greek for rushing or being borne along at speed, so 'he was carried at a ram' is how the language says he came down on it headlong. The jackdaw is proverbially the bird that apes its betters.

sentences.t: Ἐμπαρέντων δὲ αὐτοῦ τῶν ὀνύχων τοῖς μάλλοις, ἐξαρθῆναι μὴ δυνάμενος ἐπτερύσσετο, ἕως ὁ ποιμήν, τὸ γεγονὸς αἰσθόμενος, προσδραμὼν συνέλαβεν αὐτὸν καὶ περικόψας αὐτοῦ τὰ ὀξυπτερά, ὡς ἑσπέρα κατέλαβε, τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ παισὶν ἐκόμισε.
sentences.tr: Emparentōn de autou tōn onychōn tois mallois, exarthēnai mē dynamenos epterysseto, heōs ho poimēn, to gegonos aisthomenos, prosdramōn synelaben auton kai perikopsas autou ta oxyptera, hōs hespera katelabe, tois heautou paisin ekomise.
sentences.l: And his claws having been caught fast in the fleece, being unable to be lifted off, he kept fluttering, until the shepherd, having perceived the thing that had happened, having run up, seized him, and having clipped his sharp-feathers, when evening came on, brought him to his own children.
sentences.i: His claws caught fast in the fleece, and unable to lift off he beat his wings, until the shepherd, seeing what had happened, ran up and caught him; and having clipped his wing-tips, he brought him home to his children when evening came on.
sentences.n: Ἐμπαρέντων is the aorist passive participle of ἐμπείρω, 'to pierce into, be fixed in' — a rare form, here in yet another genitive absolute. τὸ γεγονός, 'the thing that has happened,' is the perfect participle doing duty as a noun. τὰ ὀξυπτερά, 'the sharp-feathers,' are the long pinion feathers that make flight possible; clipping them is what turns a wild bird into a plaything for the children.

sentences.t: Τῶν δὲ πυνθανομένων τί εἴη τὸ ὄρνεον, ἔφη.
sentences.tr: Tōn de pynthanomenōn ti eiē to orneon, ephē.
sentences.l: And they asking what the bird might be, he said.
sentences.i: When they asked what the bird was, he said:
sentences.n: A genitive absolute with the article alone as its subject: τῶν πυνθανομένων, 'they asking.' εἴη is the optative in an indirect question after a past main verb — Greek shifts the mood where English shifts the tense. Chambry prints a full stop after ἔφη and gives the speech its own line.

sentences.t: « Ὡς μὲν ἐγὼ σαφῶς οἶδα, κολοιός, ὡς δὲ αὐτὸς βούλεται, ἀετός. »
sentences.tr: « Hōs men egō saphōs oida, koloios, hōs de autos bouletai, aetos. »
sentences.l: « As I know for certain, a jackdaw; but as he himself wishes, an eagle. »
sentences.n: The joke is built entirely on μέν … δέ balanced across two ὡς-clauses, with the verb left out of both halves: 'as I know — jackdaw; as he wants — eagle.' Greek drops the copula wherever the sense supplies it, and the compression is the wit. The guillemets « » are Chambry's editorial quotation marks.

sentences.t: Οὕτως ἡ πρὸς τοὺς ὑπερέχοντας ἅμιλλα, πρὸς τῷ μηδὲν ἀνύειν, καὶ ἐπὶ συμφοραῖς προσκτᾶται γέλωτα.
sentences.tr: Houtōs hē pros tous hyperechontas hamilla, pros tōi mēden anyein, kai epi symphorais prosktatai gelōta.
sentences.l: So too rivalry against those who surpass one, besides accomplishing nothing, also gains laughter on top of misfortunes.
sentences.i: So too contending with your betters accomplishes nothing, and earns ridicule on top of the harm it brings.
sentences.n: πρὸς τῷ μηδὲν ἀνύειν is an articular infinitive: the article τῷ turns 'to accomplish nothing' into a noun that the preposition can govern — 'in addition to accomplishing nothing.' The moral opens with Οὕτως, the 'so too' that maps the story onto life, though without the καί that usually follows it. ἐπὶ συμφοραῖς: the laughter comes on top of disasters already suffered.
